Area Forecast Discussion
National Weather Service Burlington VT
219 PM EDT Wed Aug 26 2026

.WHAT HAS CHANGED...
As of 219 PM EDT Wednesday...

Confidence in isolated severe thunderstorms has increased for 
Thursday afternoon and evening.

&&

.KEY MESSAGES...
As of 219 PM EDT Wednesday...

1. Thunderstorms are increasingly likely Thursday afternoon and 
evening, with greater chances in Vermont and particularly southern 
areas. Some storms will be capable of strong winds and heavy rain. 

2. Lingering and decreasing shower and thunderstorm threat for 
Friday followed by beautiful weather to start the weekend.

3. Unsettled weather with increasing chances for precipitation 
expected for early next week. 

&&

.DISCUSSION...
As of 219 PM EDT Wednesday...

KEY MESSAGE 1: 

Likelihood of numerous showers and thunderstorms for Thursday 
afternoon and evening continues to increase today in portions of 
northern New York and Vermont. Big picture: isolated severe 
thunderstorms areawide remain possible east of the St. Lawrence 
Valley. If confidence in location and intensity of thunderstorms 
increases tonight, this outlook could very well change. Strong 
moisture advection will occur ahead of a cold front with well 
aligned southwesterly flow and mainly southerly winds at the 
surface. Plenty of solar heating to start the day concurrent with 
the incoming trough cooling temperatures aloft will aid in 
blossoming instability. MLCAPE will surge into the 1000-1500 J/kg 
range across the Champlain Valley and central Vermont during the 
afternoon as surface temperatures and dew points will likely be in 
excess of 80 and 60. About 30-35 knots of deep layer shear and 
similar effective shear will likely be present. Overall, the 
CAPE/shear balance appears to be sufficient for some stronger 
variety thunderstorms and possible low-topped supercells to form. 

In our region, the most likely timing for thunderstorms, including 
isolated severe storms, appears to be from about 4 to 8 PM. The 
greatest risk area is somewhat uncertain, but favors the region from 
the eastern Adirondacks into at least the western half of Vermont. 
Storm initiation may be upstream in central or eastern New York 
earlier in the afternoon where the best instability will be located, 
with cells moving parallel to the flow towards the northeast into 
our region coincident with a warm front. This boundary will help 
winds turn to more of a southeasterly flow near the surface across 
the southern Champlain Valley into portions of central Vermont; with 
some low level convergent flow along with terrain-generated lift, 
storms may tend to strengthen during the evening as 0-1 km storm 
relative helicity increases. The low level spin/veering winds will 
aid in organized, stronger storms that could be more long lived than 
a typical thunderstorm. All hazards with these storms are on the 
table, with the most likely one being straight line winds. The 
greater the instability, the more likely these hazards come to 
fruition. At this time, a greater risk/more coverage of stronger 
storms is favored south of our region per consensus of both the 
physically-based and machine learning model guidance.

There is also a localized flash flood threat with this event, 
particularly in the evening and in south central/western portions of 
Vermont. While precipitable water will not be particularly high, 
values in excess of 1.5" and/or 85th percentile for the time of year 
will be sufficient for heavy rain. Additionally, integrated vapor 
transport from the southwest coincident with deep moisture will be 
present. Some CAMs show a plausible, but unlikely, scenario in which 
multi-cell thunderstorms that had been propagating southeastward 
stall out for a couple of hours, repeatedly moving over the same 
areas and producing locally 2+ inches of rainfall within three 
hours. Some slight pressure rises and pause in height falls are 
noted during this period, which can contribute to stalling of 
convection that was previously moving along. There remains mixed 
signals among CAMs during the latest model cycle on this potential, 
so confidence is fairly low on flash flooding, but note training 
thunderstorms are possible if ingredients line up.

KEY MESSAGE 2: Deep moisture will be shunted to our east by Friday 
morning. As such, the only limited thunderstorm potential will be 
tied to the lingering surface cold front which will most likely be 
passing uneventfully through the region during the morning. It 
appears it will get hung up just enough over southern Vermont that a 
small window during the afternoon hours where showers develop along 
the boundary exists such that a thunderstorm is possible in south 
central to southeastern portions of the state, especially if these 
areas break out into some sunshine. Abundant dry air aloft points to 
widely scattered showers, so only a very select few locations will 
see hazardous weather as showers will struggle to produce lightning. 
Thunderstorm probabilities have fallen into the 10 to 13% range in 
southern/eastern portions of Vermont (contrasted with 30-40% in much 
of the area on Thursday). Following any convective activity during 
the afternoon, a very pleasant air mass will continue advecting in 
from the northwest Friday night setting the stage for a gorgeous, 
sunny day with low humidity for Saturday as ridging builds in at the 
surface and aloft. High temperatures should be very seasonable, 
ranging through the 70s.

KEY MESSAGE 3: High pressure will slide to our east on Sunday, and at 
this point, expect the second half of the weekend to be mainly dry. 
Uncertainty grows thereafter as an upper trough swings across Quebec 
and into northern/eastern New England, sweeping a cold front along 
its wake. There remains considerable spread in model solutions with 
this system, particularly how far southward the front makes it 
before possibly lifting back north as a warm front as low pressure 
slides to our north. For example, the 12z GFS solution sets up the 
front directly over our region, with waves of low pressure to slide 
along it from later Sunday into mid week. The result is a period of 
particularly wet and cooler weather. Do note the GEFS ensembles 
don't support the operational solution, with 24-hr probabilities of 
greater than a half inch of rainfall remaining fairly low. 
Meanwhile, the 00z ECMWF isn't so dire, lifting the cold front back 
to our north Monday into Tuesday, keeping rounds of showers more 
transient and allowing us to warm back up into the 80s by mid week. 
Have not made changes to the NBM from Sunday onward given the 
uncertainty, but it'll be interesting to see how trends play out as 
we draw closer to next week.

&&

.AVIATION /18Z WEDNESDAY THROUGH MONDAY/...
Through 18Z Thursday...VFR conditions will prevail for much of the
TAF period with fair weather cumulus remaining SCT AOA 3500 ft
through this evening. Clouds dissipate toward sunset, with a few
mid/high clouds expected overnight. Patchy fog will be possible late
tonight/early Thursday morning, mainly along the favored river
valleys in eastern VT. Periods of IFR/LIFR conditions are expected
due to fog at MPV 08z-12z Thu, with less confidence of 
significant impacts at EFK. Clouds increase again after 12z Thu 
ahead of an approaching frontal boundary, but VFR should prevail
with shower/thunderstorm development holding off until late in 
and/or after this forecast period. Winds generally 5 kt or less 
this afternoon and overnight. Only exception will be a SE lake 
breeze at PBG, where sustained winds will remain closer to 10 kt
until 23z. Winds will begin to increase later tonight and 
especially during the daylight hours on Thu. Expect S/SW winds 
around 10 kt with gusts of 16-20 kt.

Outlook...

Thursday Night: VFR. Chance SHRA, Slight chance TSRA.
Friday: Mainly VFR, with local MVFR possible. Chance SHRA, Slight
chance TSRA.
Friday Night: VFR. NO SIG WX.
Saturday: VFR. NO SIG WX.
Saturday Night: VFR. NO SIG WX.
Sunday: VFR. NO SIG WX.
Sunday Night: Mainly VFR, with areas MVFR possible. Chance SHRA.
Monday: Mainly MVFR, with local IFR possible. Chance SHRA, Slight
chance TSRA.

&&

.BTV WATCHES/WARNINGS/ADVISORIES...
VT...None.
NY...None.

&&

$$
